bodyMarkdown:
## Emerging products as an origination context

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Emerging product work is defined by origination. The characteristic challenge is to build product structure for the first time, not to improve an existing structure. In this context, information architecture starts before any interface exists: entities, relationships, user journeys, scope boundaries, and product logic have to be made explicit before interaction design can stabilise.

The translation problem in emerging products is often the movement from domain expertise to product model. The available knowledge may be directionally strong but not yet structured as a product. In Creative Navy's vocabulary, this is the blanks phenomenon: founder or stakeholder intuition may be correct, but the value, structure, or interaction logic cannot yet be named as a product.

Emerging product work is commonly shaped by bootstrapped constraints. Timelines and budgets can be compressed, and the prototype may become the primary communication artefact for investors, commissioners, partners, or early adopters. In pre-revenue or pre-deployment situations, the prototype is often the product for the audience that must decide whether the product should be funded, commissioned, built, or purchased.

## Domain learning before an operational product exists

Domain learning in emerging products does not usually come from an established operational system. It can come from a founder's or researcher's materials, from stakeholder and beneficiary knowledge, or from a published standards corpus supplied by the client.

In Greenlight, the starting material was a doctoral researcher's thesis about how workplace safety incidents are recorded, escalated, and followed up in real organisations. The thesis contained implicit structure: categories, severity scales, near-miss events, escalation paths, and follow-up actions. Creative Navy's first phase of work was to extract that structure, validate it with the domain expert, and make it explicit as a product model.

In Neugo, domain learning came from the Home Office and four legal firms rather than from a single founder's corpus. The first engagement had no deployed system, no user base, and no operational evidence to read. The task was to make a UK visa application case-management platform concrete enough to support a public commissioning decision.

In Topera, domain learning came from a published standards corpus supplied by the client: DIN 69901 parts 1–5, the ProSTEP iViP CPM Reference Model, the ProSTEP iViP Data Exchange Model, the ProSTEP iViP / VDA schedule management recommendation, and the ProSTEP iViP PSMS recommendation. This is the opposite source class to a founder's thesis. A thesis may be incomplete and require extraction; a formal standards corpus is complete, formal, and exhaustive, and the design task becomes subtraction under judgement.

## Information architecture at origination

Information architecture at origination defines the product's structure before the product has a stable interface. Creative Navy's emerging product work uses option space mapping at the architecture level when there is no existing system to analyse. The option space is opened structurally before detailed interaction design begins.

In Greenlight, Creative Navy explored three information architecture concepts: a linear flow, a modular architecture with conditional sections, and intermediate variants. The concepts were compared across minor incidents, serious injuries, and near-miss reports. The convergence decision was a modular architecture with a consistent spine and conditional sections.

In Topera, the information architecture was built as a two-axis matrix. The horizontal time axis carried the five DIN 69901-2 lifecycle phases: Initialisation, the DIN 69901-2 Definition phase, Planning, Execution and Monitoring, and Closure. The vertical knowledge axis carried eleven management domains: project structure, schedule and milestones, communication and reporting, cost and budget, human resources, resources, quality, risk, contract, deliverables, and change management.

Every Topera matrix cell was populated with three elements: the DIN 69901-2 processes active in that phase, the DIN 69901-4 data model entities that carry the information, and the PSI 25 synchronisation activity that propagates it to partners. The design specification traced standard elements to screens, modules, actions, and scope tiers. This was a standards-grounded architecture exercise, not a conformance, certification, or compliance claim.

## Prototype as the primary communication artefact

In emerging product contexts, the prototype often has to make an opportunity legible to people who cannot evaluate the product from a description alone. The audience may be private investors, public commissioners, consortium stakeholders, or buyers deciding whether a technical premise is commercially credible.

In Greenlight, Creative Navy delivered an interactive prototype in approximately 4 weeks, assembled an investor demo in approximately 1 week, and documented the work for development handover. Those delivery facts are Creative Navy-observed. No post-engagement data on investor conversations, funding, or deployment is available for publication.

In Veecle, client-reported evidence records that £2M development funding was unlocked. The designs were used in investor demonstrations where the interface comprised approximately 70% of the pitch content. The designs were implemented by Veecle's development team, according to client-reported evidence.

In Neugo, the clickable Figma prototype and value/desirability mapping were aimed at a public commissioning decision rather than a private investment decision. Client-reported evidence described the design as contributing roughly 30% of the decision factors, with dedicated demo sessions built around the prototype. The appropriate framing is contribution to a commissioning decision, not a claim that the design secured the commission.

## Sparse prior art and new interaction models

Sparse prior art changes the design problem in emerging products. When a product category is genuinely new, design cannot simply borrow established interaction patterns. Proposals have to generate reference points and test what the problem requires.

Puraite was an AI-assisted systematic literature review tool in a category where no direct prior art existed. Rayyan used AI as an add-on to conventional review, and Elicit used an AI-first model outside the formal systematic review process. Puraite required design for a new interaction model rather than adaptation of an established one.

The Puraite engagement had no user research access available while a beta launch was being prepared. Creative Navy used the Creative Navy PM's firsthand systematic review experience as a domain learning proxy, and presented the tradeoffs and limitations of that methodological choice to the client.

Creative Navy ran four iterations on the AI suggestion display before resolving the tension between compact scanning and enough detail to support override. The resolution was to make a direct quote from the publication visible in the side panel from the outset, with no interaction required to access supporting evidence. Creative Navy also reduced navigation from 13 top-level items to 4; the client described this as one of the most significant contributions of the engagement.

## Boundary cases that still contain origination work

Not every relevant engagement is a full greenfield emerging product. Some cases sit at the boundary because the product existed technically, or because origination occurred inside a broader redesign engagement.

Hudex v2 was a platform pivot from a social media analysis tool to a general-purpose intelligence operating platform. The project overview page required 20 iterations, the highest count across any single component in that engagement. The concept had to be invented rather than refined, and the resulting project overview functioned as origination work within a broader redesign engagement. Client-reported evidence records £3M investment received 3 months into the growth phase, with the client attributing the design as critical and foundational.

Squaremind was technically real but commercially dormant. The hardware worked, the robot arm scanned, and the software processed images. The commercial challenge was that Squaremind's autonomous patient-operation premise had not been demonstrated: Squaremind's own pre-redesign test with 14 patients produced 2 completions, according to client-reported background evidence.

Creative Navy's work in Squaremind was not to build a product model. It was to build a guidance architecture for a sequential physical process with no tolerance for unrecovered confusion. The Inform–Prevent–Correct framework was produced during Concept Convergence and mapped step by step across the scan flow. Post-redesign ecological testing across two sites recorded 27 of 29 patients completing the scan independently, and all 12 patients who got stuck recovered. The commercial outcome was client-reported: all 9 clinics purchased, and Creative Navy observed 5 of 9 demos.

## Topera as standards-governed concept design with no outcome claim

Topera is the first industrial, standards-governed instance in this emerging-products set. It is a concept design for a cross-organisational project management platform grounded in the DIN 69901 series and the ProSTEP iViP / VDA recommendations. Topera is not a built product, not a deployed system, not a pilot, and not a product with users.

Topera's scope was set by synchronisation depth rather than by feature list. SL1.1 and SL1.2 were required, SL2.1 and SL2.2 were target scope, SL2.3 was stretch, and SL3.x was post-MVP. The same ladder was applied to CPM collaboration classes, with CC1 to CC3 in scope and CC4 deferred. This drew the MVP boundary against an external, published, verifiable yardstick rather than an internal feature list.

The architecture covered all fourteen DIN 69901-2 Mindeststandard processes: the fourteen of DIN 69901-2's fifty-nine processes designated as the minimum set every project must run. Each appeared by its standard process code in the architecture mapping and design requirements documents. This is a coverage check only. It does not show that the processes were well designed, that coverage is adequate for a build, or that any assessment took place. Creative Navy certified to no standard, audited against none, and worked to none.

The Topera concept also illustrates standards-to-interface translation. DIN 69901-4 treats the Vorhaben as the central entity and uses one polymorphic entity type for a project, work package, activity, and milestone, distinguished by a type attribute and nested through a sub-initiative relationship. That data-model reading licensed one tree view carrying four kinds of thing rather than four separate surfaces. The same reading supported a Gantt concept with configurable information columns for different readers.

Creative Navy scoped a full design of the platform at twenty-four one-week sprints and put that position to the client before the engagement began. The client commissioned three one-week sprints as a concept design. The twenty-four-sprint figure is Creative Navy's professional estimate of the full scope, not a measured comparison between two pieces of work. Topera's team was pleased with the concept design and took it to show stakeholders. No stakeholder response, decision, commitment, funding event, performance result, adoption result, revenue result, or commercial outcome is known to Creative Navy, and none is claimed.

## Evidence boundaries in emerging product examples

The emerging-products evidence set mixes Creative Navy-observed engagement facts, client-reported outcomes, Creative Navy-recorded design decisions, and case-specific measured or ecological testing. The evidence should not be read as a uniform measurement set.

Greenlight demonstrates Creative Navy's capability in a specific mode: working with domain experts who are not yet product thinkers, extracting implicit structure from non-product sources, and producing credible artefacts under bootstrapped constraints. It should not be presented as representative of Creative Navy's typical engagement complexity.

Puraite's post-redesign evidence is a client-reported product-legitimacy shift: users who had perceived Puraite as theoretical began actively using it, and the client entered a growth phase. It is not a measured performance improvement.

Neugo is the only origination case in this set with downstream deployment evidence. The originated concept was carried through a full build and a post-launch audit into a live system that 15 legal firms were relying on at the audit, having begun replacing some of their internal processes with its features. That reliance validates the built product, not the origination work alone, because the path from origination vision to operational reliance ran through a separate build engagement.

Topera has the strictest boundary. No research finding, user insight, usability result, observed behaviour, client decision, stakeholder response, compliance credential, or business outcome exists for Topera. The correct evidence claim is that a concept design was produced from a client-supplied standards corpus and that its architecture carried traceable standard references and synchronisation levels.

## Related pages

The Greenlight, Puraite, Squaremind, and Topera pages provide case-level examples that connect to the emerging-products context. Related context pages include AI-enabled products, government and public sector, regulated products, enterprise software, expert tools and internal systems, and industrial automation and machinery where those contexts overlap with the specific conditions described here.
